title: One Overlooked Reason the Democrats May Have Won the Midterms
summary: Is humility poised for a political comeback?

On the morning after his astonishing 12-point win in one of the most closely watched Senate races in decades, James Talarico, a newly minted Democratic superstar from a newly blue Texas, visited a patch of red. He went on Fox News.


He could have been walking into the lion’s den as a show of mettle or simply to gloat. Before Election Day, he’d been[mocked](https://ca.news.yahoo.com/jesse-watters-snidely-attacks-james-134019795.html) on the network as James “Tala-freak-o,” and here he was, a freaky and fantabulous victor getting the last laugh.


But when I watched his conversation with the anchors Dana Perino and Bill Hemmer, I didn’t get the impression that he was there to celebrate his own triumph. What struck me, as it has over the past year, was Talarico’s reserve and restraint.


He urged people[not to listen](https://x.com/Breaking911/status/2117993700177346674?a=NSuYwy4KbCWB-Sxr5WA&s=20) to him — or any other politician — too closely, because words are easy and actions count more. He not only[complimented](https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/fox-news-bill-hemmer-dana-172020682.html) President Trump on securing the nation’s Southern border, but also eschewed too much talk of prosecuting officials in the Trump administration. “I am not interested in retribution,” he said. He told Texans who hadn’t voted for him that he’d be working hard for them nonetheless.


I might dismiss all of that as pretty blather if it weren’t so consistent with his tone over time. And I wouldn’t linger over it and thrill to it if it didn’t reflect a faint pattern I detected in many Democrats’ successful midterm campaigns. I saw shoots of humility on a political landscape that has been largely barren of it over recent years.


A lack of humility explains a whole lot about our dysfunction and divisiveness, which we won’t repair without[a resurgence of it](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/04/20/opinion/students-humility-american-politics.html?searchResultPosition=15) . We’ve been at one another’s throats in part because we’ve been unhumble — and thus unable to acknowledge that there might be good reason for someone’s divergent opinion, that it’s not necessary to win every argument, that the public good matters as much as our private satisfaction and that a healthy democracy requires compromise, forgiveness, grace. We’ve had unhumble governments, and that has intensified partisanship and exacerbated its toll.
